subject: music
title: Theory Application: Scales, Keys & Intervals
welcome_lead: Get hands-on with the patterns that shape melodies — scales, keys and intervals.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Theory Adventure 2: applying scale patterns, key signatures, intervals and the circle of fifths.
final_note: You can now build scales, recognise keys and measure intervals at speed.

concepts.def: Five-note scale, common in folk and blues.
Sharps or flats at the start that fix the key.
Distance between two notes, measured in steps.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Start on any note and follow the pattern T-T-S-T-T-T-S. From C: C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C — all white notes. From G: G-A-B-C-D-E-F♯-G (one sharp).

The circle of fifths shows how each new key adds one sharp (clockwise) or one flat (anti-clockwise).

Major scales sound bright and happy. Minor scales sound darker. Each major key has a relative minor using the same notes — A minor is the relative minor of C major (no sharps/flats).

Other shapes: pentatonic (5 notes, used in folk/rock solos) and chromatic (all 12 semitones — often decorative).

walkthroughs.h2: Counting from one note to another
walkthroughs.body_html:
Count both notes inclusively: C to E spans C-D-E = a 3rd. C to G spans 5 notes = a 5th. C to C spans 8 = an octave.

Intervals are also major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished depending on the exact distance in semitones.
